result.summary: No part of the 2^32 at C3 can be removed by partial evaluation, reordering or merging with C2, or by using the collapsed condition to prune the a3 lookup. Every bit of c3 depends on every bit of a3 (sensitivity matrix has no zero entry, min 0.089); c3 mod 2^k is a3-dependent for all k>=1; the GF(2) span of c3 differences under a3 has rank 32 and the joint (c2,c3) span rank 64, so no linear (GF(2) or modular) functional of c3, or of any combination of the C2 and C3 residuals, is a3-free; two roots of the same C2 key give c3 values agreeing at 0.499 per bit, so the key carries no information about c3 before the lookup. The collapse condition fixes ~16 scattered bits of a3 before the C2 lookup, but modular carries in W3 = a3 + F23 mean only a trailing forced block L>=19 yields a sound pre-lookup test (L-18 key bits), which skips 1.6e-6 of C2 lookups (model 2^-19 * 2/3), verified sound on 451 collapse survivors; the known half of a3 predicts c3 at 49.8% per bit. Lookup accounting on the real table: 1.000 + 0.6337 + 0.4016 = 2.035 lookups per swept a0; realisable saving ~3e-7 of lookups; even removing every C2 lookup would be only 1.25x. Gain in bits: 0.
result.mechanism: Blocking dependency: a3 enters W4 through Sigma0(a3) (in T2^(4)) and through Sigma1(e3) and Ch(e3,e2,e1) with e3 = a_{-1} + a3 - T2^(3); Sigma0 and Sigma1 are one-input rotation-XOR maps with nothing to saturate, and with the carries of e3 = a3 + const and of the modular sum in W4 they make every W4 bit, hence every sigma0(W4) bit (bit i = W4[i+3]^W4[i+7]^W4[i+18]), hence every bit of c3 = sigma0(W4) + W3 - kappa3, depend on every a3 bit. C2's only a3-dependence is sigma0(W3) - W3 with W3 = a3 + F23, C3's is sigma0(W4(a3)) + a3; sigma0 is GF(2)-linear but not Z/2^32-linear and W4 is not affine in a3, so no combination of the two residuals cancels a3 (joint difference span rank 64/64). For the collapse pre-filter, the carry chain of W3 = a3 + F23 destroys the ~16 scattered forced bits; only a trailing forced run of length L fixes W3 mod 2^L, and sigma0(W3) - W3 mod 2^k needs W3 bits up to k+17, so the test exists only for L >= 19 (probability 2^-19) and is worth 2^-19 * 2/3 of C2 lookups.

C3 itself is friendly: it can be written as a one-input form in six of the eight words — a4: σ0(W4)−W4 (global); a5: +a5 exactly linear (a7=a6, e11=0; verified 200/200 at full width); a6: +a6 exactly linear (a7=a5, e11=-1; 200/200); a7: Σ1(a7+c11)−Σ0(a7) (per-context, from e8 and e11 in W12); a8: x−Σ0(x) global; a9: σ1(x)+x global (x=W17=c−a9, using σ1(W17) and −e9 in W12 with a10=a8, e11=0); a10, a11: never (σ1(W17) contains Maj(A12,a11,a10)/Maj(A13,A12,a11) and Ch(e16,·,·) with digest words that cannot be equated or saturated). result.plain_english: The attack works by guessing one 32-bit word (a0) and then reading three unknown words off a precomputed table, one per equation; the fourth equation is a 32-bit check that either passes or fails, with no information available beforehand about which. The question was whether any structure could let us skip part of that check. Seven teams tried every route we could think of: absorbing a different word with the fourth equation, building a second table, changing which word is guessed and which are looked up, evaluating the check partially, merging it with the third equation, tying the context to the guess, and reusing one batch of candidates for several contexts. Every route runs into the same wall. In SHA-256 each word a_k is fed, five rounds later, into the message-recovery formula through Sigma0(a_k), a one-input scrambling function. With a two-input function you can sometimes fix one input to a constant that makes the other input irrelevant; with a one-input function there is nothing to fix, so the only way to make it harmless is to already know a_k. At 20 rounds there are twelve free words and four equations; three equations are already spoken for (a1 can only be recovered from the first, a2 from the second, a3 from the third), and whichever word the fourth equation would recover reaches one of the first three through such a one-input function. That closes the loop, and the cheapest way to break the loop is the one the paper already uses, which costs the 2^13.4 factor; the 2^32 is the fourth equation itself, and it cannot be shrunk because the quantities it tests are already completely determined by the guess. Two thousand planted solutions and a full run of an alternative arrangement with the real table match this accounting exactly. The honest conclusion is that this line is closed: the published 2^45.4 is the best any table-absorption frame can do at 20 rounds, and the only remaining untested ideas lie outside the family of tricks the attack is built from and have no structural reason to work.
